summary: Defines the Port Control Protocol, which lets an IPv4 or IPv6 host control how incoming packets are translated and forwarded by a NAT or simple firewall. It also lets a host reduce its outgoing NAT keepalive messages.

plainLanguage.summary: PCP lets a host ask a NAT or firewall to forward selected incoming traffic. It also reports how long a mapping lasts, so a client can renew it or notice when the server has lost its state.

subtitle: A host protocol for requesting port mappings and learning how long NAT or firewall state will last.

tldr.problem: A host behind a NAT or firewall may not receive incoming traffic, and applications may send repeated packets just to keep mappings active.
tldr.mechanism: PCP sends UDP requests to create, renew, or delete mappings, or to learn and extend an outbound mapping for a specific remote peer.
tldr.outcome: PCP also lets clients detect server state loss and restore mappings. RFC 6887 has been updated by RFC 7488, RFC 7652 and RFC 7843.

today: RFC 6887 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7488, RFC 7652 and RFC 7843.

sections.title: What PCP Is For
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP) lets an IPv4 or IPv6 host control how a NAT or simple firewall translates and forwards packets. It can create mappings that allow incoming traffic to reach an internal host, and it can help reduce application keepalive traffic.

PCP does not tell remote computers how to find a new mapping. An application uses its own rendezvous method for that purpose. The RFC assumes a single-homed network, where traffic from a host uses one default route so replies return through the same NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: PCP lets a host request a path for incoming traffic through a NAT or firewall. The application still has to tell remote systems how to use that path.

sections.title: Requests as Hints and Responses as Updates
sections.content:
PCP can be understood as two related message streams. A client sends hints describing the mapping state it wants, and the server sends responses describing the state that exists. Because the response describes the mapping, PCP does not use a transaction identifier.

PCP messages use UDP and have a maximum payload of 1100 octets. The client handles retransmission when a response is missing, using the same Mapping Nonce for retransmissions. A response can also arrive without an immediately preceding request when the server reports a mapping change.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a request describing the mapping it wants. The server reports what it did, and may later send an update if that state changes.

sections.title: The Common Message Header
sections.content:
Every PCP message has a common header, an Opcode-specific payload, and optional options. Version 2 is specified here. A request includes an Opcode, requested lifetime, and the client's 128-bit IP address. IPv4 addresses use an IPv4-mapped IPv6 representation.

A response includes a result code, a lifetime, and an Epoch Time. The client address in a request lets the server detect a NAT between the client and the PCP-controlled device. Options use a type, length, and value format; an option with its high bit clear is mandatory to process.
sections.plainLanguage: The common header identifies the request type and the client's address. A response reports whether the request worked and how long the resulting state lasts.

sections.title: MAP and PEER Operations
sections.content:
MAP creates or renews an explicit dynamic inbound mapping between an internal address, protocol, and port and an external address, protocol, and port. A zero requested lifetime asks to delete the mapping. The client may suggest an external address and port, but it must be prepared for the server to assign different values.

PEER creates or extends an outbound mapping to a particular remote peer. It can report the external address, port, and lifetime for that mapping, helping an application reduce keepalive messages. PEER cannot shorten or delete a mapping. Both operations use a 96-bit Mapping Nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: MAP requests an incoming mapping for a host. PEER requests information or more time for an outbound mapping to a particular remote system.

sections.title: Options and Mapping Lifetimes
sections.content:
THIRD_PARTY allows an authorized client to request a mapping for another internal host, but MUST NOT be implemented or used unless the network carrying PCP messages is fully trusted. PREFER_FAILURE asks a MAP server not to create an alternative mapping if it cannot use the suggested external address and port. FILTER restricts which remote addresses and ports may send packets through a MAP mapping.

Mappings have a finite lifetime, which the client must renew to keep them. A server SHOULD support configurable minimum and maximum lifetimes; the recommended minimum is 120 seconds and the suggested maximum, if no better information exists, is 24 hours.
sections.plainLanguage: Options can request a mapping for another host, require an exact external port, or limit which remote systems can send traffic. A client renews a mapping before its lifetime ends.

sections.title: Detecting Server State Loss
sections.content:
Every response includes an Epoch Time that normally increases once per second. A server MUST reset the Epoch if it loses mapping state or its external address changes. A client compares Epoch values and its own clock to detect a reset or a clock difference outside the permitted tolerance.

When the client detects an anomalous Epoch, it promptly renews its active mappings. A server that may lose state or change mappings MUST implement either ANNOUNCE or Mapping Update and SHOULD implement both. ANNOUNCE can notify clients after a restart; Mapping Update reports changed external addresses or ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The Epoch Time helps a client notice when the server has restarted or lost mapping state. The client can then renew its mappings instead of waiting for their regular renewal time.

sections.title: Threat Models and Security Limits
sections.content:
The Simple Threat Model protects against off-path attackers, but not an attacker who can modify, drop, or inject spoofed packets on the internal network. Under this model, a server must not create explicit mappings it would not allow implicitly; the RFC gives single administrative control, matching lifetimes, and no THIRD_PARTY support as conditions.

The Advanced Threat Model requires an authenticated, integrity-protected signaling channel, which RFC 6887 does not specify. Remaining risks include denial of service through resource exhaustion, on-path interference, and mapping theft during recovery. The RFC recommends ingress filtering and per-host or per-subscriber mapping quotas.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic model protects against attackers who are not on the path, within stated limits. The RFC does not define the secure signaling mechanism needed for more demanding deployments.
